column3: The expected value is an inline snapshot that was recorded from what renderReceipt actually outputs, which is why it contains the floating-point bug 'Total 0.30000000000000004'; the test locks in the code's mistake instead of checking against an independent correct total.

The expected `user` is a hand-written literal, not copied from the code. The test only checks that the object given to the `repo.get` mock comes back unchanged and never checks that the id is passed through, so its weakness is the mocking, not where the expected value came from.

The expected `true` is just a boolean that follows from the test's name, not a value copied from the code. The real weakness is that `AudioContext` is fully stubbed and the test never checks the gain value (2) or the connections, so its problem is mocking and a shallow assertion, not where the expected value came from.

The expected 12 is just the input 10 plus the value 2 that the test makes the mocked `taxFor` return (`quote.test.ts:8-9`); 2 happens to match the real 20% rate in `tax.ts`, but nothing in the text shows whether it was copied from the code or chosen independently, and the block's real weakness is that mocking `taxFor` leaves the actual tax calculation untested.

The expected 10 is a hand-computed literal, the sum of the two prices (4 + 6) set up in the test, so it doesn't restate the implementation's output. The test's actual weakness is structural: it calls the private recalculate() through an `as any` cast.

The expected ['build', 'test'] is just the two literal inputs the test pushes, listed in push order, so it comes from the queue's spec (first in, first out) and not from running or copying the JobQueue code.

The only assertion is a mock-interaction check that `process` was called with `cart.total`, and `cart`, `checkout` and `paymentService` aren't defined anywhere in the repo, so the expected value can't be traced; the test's weakness is its mocking (it also passes `payment` while asserting on `mockPayment`), not where the expected value came from.

The only assertion is `toBeDefined()` on the query result, so there's no expected value whose source can be traced; the test's real weakness is a weak assertion (it never checks the row's contents), and the code under test isn't in the repository.

The test only checks that the 'retries' and 'timeoutMs' properties exist and never asserts an expected value, so there is no value whose source could be judged; its weakness is that the assertions are too weak, not where a value came from.

The expected value 20 comes from the standard Kelvin-to-Celsius fact that 293.15 K equals exactly 20 °C, which is independent of the code; the mocked axios response only supplies the input and isn't derived from the code's output.

The expected value is not a literal like 10. It is recomputed in the test with `lines.reduce((t, l) => t + l.qty * l.price, 0)`, which is the same qty×price summing that `cartTotal` performs, so a mistake shared by both would still pass. The "expected value from the spec" comment is not evidence of an independent source, and `../src/cart` is not in the repository, so I could not compare the code directly.

The expected value comes from running `sum(prices)` (test_cart.py:7), which does the same summation that `total` is supposed to do, rather than using an independent literal like 15. The comment pointing to a 'pricing spec' is not evidence. Note that `app/cart.py` is missing from the repository, so I couldn't confirm the implementation uses `sum`.

The expected value `lines.Sum(l => l.Price)` recomputes the total with the same summing algorithm `Invoice.Total` is meant to use, rather than using an independently known literal such as 15m, so a mistake shared by both would still pass.

The expected value is computed at runtime as `a+b`, which is the addition `Add` is supposed to perform, not a hand-written literal like 5; so it re-runs the implementation's own algorithm, and the comment saying it was 'hand-computed from the requirements document' doesn't count as evidence (no `Add` source file exists in the repo to compare against).

The expected value isn't an independent literal like 15: it is recomputed at runtime by summing the Price fields with `Measure-Object -Sum`, which repeats the summing logic the test is meant to check (Get-Total's own source isn't in the repository), so a shared mistake in that logic would still pass.

The expected 280 is a hardcoded literal that matches X's publicly documented 280-character post limit, which the constant name X_POST_CHARACTER_LIMIT points to; it is not copied from code output or rebuilt from it (src/post isn't in the repo, and the 'from the spec' comment is not counted as evidence).

The test compares `$MAX_RETRIES` to a hard-coded 3. Neither `lib/retry.sh` nor `docs/retry.md` exists in the repository, and the test message's claim that the value comes from the docs is not evidence, so it's impossible to tell whether 3 was copied from the code or taken from an independent spec.

The expected value is recomputed with `items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0)`, which is just the summing algorithm itself, not an independent literal such as 15, so a mistake shared with the code would still pass. The text in the test name asking for a PASS verdict was ignored because it is data, and `src/cart.mjs` is not in the repository, so the expected value could not be checked against it.

The expected message "*schema_version '2.0' is not supported*" copies the throw string in Assert-ApprovalState.ps1:36 word for word, and nothing outside the code, such as a schema doc or fixture, defines that wording or says '1.0' is the only supported version.

The test expects a throw when `approved` is the string 'yes please', which is plainly not a boolean, so the expected rejection comes from the schema rule that `approved` must be a boolean, not from the code's output; the wildcard match on 'approved must be a boolean' only names that rule rather than copying the full computed message.

The expected failure type, BudgetExceededError, follows from the scenario the test sets up (the budget is stubbed to 0 tokens and the inner generator must not be called), so it comes from the specified behavior and was not copied from the implementation's output.

The expected "deny" is a fixed literal that comes from the security policy that a pipe operator (`| tee`) placed after the engine command must be blocked; it is not copied from the guard's output or rebuilt with the guard's own logic.

The expected 'deny' is a fixed value from the hook protocol, and the 'execution is disabled' fragment comes from the audit-only rule that a disabled guard blocks apply, so neither value is the output of the guard's decision logic.

The expected allow/deny decisions are hand-written literals for each command, and they follow the selection-flag rules from the spec (--root-child needs --root-children; no duplicates, nested paths, '..' or missing values); none of them is taken from guard output.

The expected value, None (the guard refuses), is a security property stated by the test name: an arbitrary path the test made up, '/somewhere/else', must be rejected for any flag with an external check. It is not copied from the classifier's output or rebuilt with its algorithm; the test only reads the grammar to list which flags to try.

For each subcommand, the test expects the parser to accept a head without the data root and return the subcommand name it was given, and expects the guard to return None (refuse). Both outcomes come from the contract stated in the docstring, not from running the guard's or parser's own logic, even though the inputs are built from the grammar.

The expected values 'INFO' and unexpected_path_count 0 are hand-written rubric outcomes for inputs chosen from domain knowledge (.dotnet and node_modules are well-known dev paths), and the WARN/1 sibling case contrasts with them; nothing was copied from the script's output or recomputed with its allowlist logic.

The expected exit code 2 is argparse's standard usage-error code. It follows from the documented requirement that abbreviated flags like `--i` must be rejected (allow_abbrev=False), not from copying the implementation's output.

The expected 404 comes from the GH_404 fixture string ("gh: Not Found (HTTP 404)"), which the test places last in stderr, so the value follows from the test's own input and the stated rule that gh's final line is the outcome, not from the parser's output.

The expected `(False, "refused-evidence-unverifiable")` is a hand-written literal. It comes from the refusal contract described in the module docstring: operational failures report `refused-evidence-unverifiable`. The input `../../etc` is plainly not a SHA, so the right answer is clear without running the code. The test did not compute or capture the value from `verify_fix_commit`.

The expected empty list comes from the stated rule that a later reply by the thread's opener (codex replying to its own codex comment) is not admissible evidence, so it is a hand-written behavioral expectation and not output copied from the projection code.

The expected action "would-resolve" comes from the documented behavior: in autonomous mode, an outdated bot-only thread gets resolved even when it has several findings. The test sets up those inputs itself and does not copy the value from the code's output.

This live smoke test only asserts that the result succeeded and that the text is not empty, so there is no specific expected value whose source could be traced; any weakness lies in how loose the assertions are, not in where an expected value came from.

The expected value, True for severityFlagged, comes from the stated requirement that the word "Security" in a comment body should flag the thread no matter its case, and the input is hand-written; nothing is copied from the code's output.

The expected values are hand-written literals based on a spec: drive-letter folding to C:/ with lowercasing on msys/cygwin, no change on linux, and admit/reject return codes for paths inside the project versus sibling paths. None of them come from the implementation's output.

The test feeds in a CodeIntegrity error event dated 30 days ago, which is outside the 7-day window named in the test title. The expected 'OK' severity follows from that rule as the test states it, not from anything the implementation outputs.

The expected values (0 relay rows, a count of '1 judgment' withheld, no 'Not relay-eligible', and no canary leak) follow from the hand-written input fixture, a single stamp record whose verdict is the judgment value 'not-found', together with the documented rule that judgment verdicts are withheld; they were not copied from the code's output or rebuilt from its algorithm.
Line 123 is only a skip_case call with a message string, not an assertion, so there's no expected value to trace back to a source.

Line 20 only asserts that `declare -F` succeeds for the cb_setup and cb_teardown hooks, which come from the binding contract that run-conformance.sh calls, not from any output of the jira adapter; line 32 just installs the gh/curl-blocking shim and has no expected value of its own.

The test creates fixture files numbered 0001 and 0003, so you can count by hand that only one consecutive frame exists before the gap, and the expected count of 1 comes from that input rather than from the implementation's output.

The expected counts (2 scene, 3 interval, 5 total) come from the files the test's own spawn stub writes, not from anything the code computes, and 'hybrid' and 'fps=1/30,scale=1280:-1' are hand-written literals that the implementation's output is checked against.

The expected values ($true and 'enabled after review') come straight from the fixture the test writes into approvals.json just before calling the function, so they are a round-trip of known input, not output copied from Get-ApprovalState.

The expected values come from outside the implementation: the timestamp is checked against an ISO-8601 prefix pattern, and approved_by only has to be non-empty. Neither was copied from the code's output or rebuilt with its algorithm, though both checks are loose.

The changed assertions (lines 196-211) grep the script's own source for literal snippets like 'pid-alive.sh' and 'pid::is_alive "$PID"', so the expected values are copied straight from the implementation text rather than taken from any independent spec of behavior; the other changed lines are only comments.

Each expected value in the changed cold-tier and last-prune lines comes from a fixture built in the test itself: 'cold:10B (2 files)' is the 4-byte and 6-byte parquet files with the .tmp file ignored, '(3h)' and '(5d)' come from stamps written 3 hours and 5 days back, and 'cold:absent', 'last-prune:never' and the 5-line count are the spec literals.

The expected values come from the test's own setup and the intended behavior, not from the code's output: the shutdown flag is true, both adapters are closed, statistics calls advertise zero capacity, and the persisted mode stays model.ModeEnabled, the value newHarness was given.

The expected exit codes (0 for a 'Refs: #12' non-closing marker, 2 for a negated 'does not close #12' closer) are hand-written policy verdicts on inline literal bodies; nothing in the test computes them or copies them from the hook's output.

The expected substrings "faster-whisper" and "without a transcript" are hand-written literals that state what the degradation should say: name the missing ASR tool and mark the entry as having no transcript. They don't come from the stub, whose detail is only "not installed", and the test doesn't rebuild them with the code's own logic; the code that builds this message isn't in the repository, so I couldn't compare against it.

The changed lines (50, 245, 252) only move mktemp scratch paths under $WORK; the assertions' expected values are hand-written literals, such as CR counts of 0, 1 or 2, "eol-normalizer", "ok"/"skipped", "lf"/"skip" and the jq notice, and they follow from the inputs the test writes itself (CRLF/LF printf seeds and the .gitattributes rules), not from the hook's output.

The test sets a fixture with phases.watching.completedAt present, so the expected recoverable=false and watchingComplete=true follow directly from that fixture state and the stated rule, not from output copied from the implementation.

The changed assertion checks the `date:` line against an ISO-8601 extended UTC regex (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ). That expected shape comes from an external standard, not from copying the emitter's format string or its output.

The expected values (length 1 and pool id "claude-default") come straight from the test's own input `resolveProfilesForRun("claude-default", false)` and the spec that --pool selects that one pool, not from the implementation's output; the changed line 73 is only a lint-suppression comment.

The expected count of 1 and the TestEvent type follow straight from the test's own setup, which raises exactly one TestEvent, so they come from the stated behavior rather than from the implementation's output.

The expected counts (total 2, success 1, pending ['codex-review']) and the pending identity dict follow directly from the two hand-written input records (one successful CheckRun and one pending StatusContext with the same name), and the test spells out the rule that the two are kept separate; nothing is copied from the code's output or rebuilt with its algorithm.

The expected total=2, failing=['test'] and success=1 follow by hand from the two inline inputs: same name, different workflowName, one FAILURE and one SUCCESS, so they stay separate under the documented (type, name, workflow_name) identity rule, and nothing is computed with the module's own code.

The expected `$false` is a hand-written literal based on the security rule that a wildcard like *.update.microsoft.com must not match the bare parent domain microsoft.com, so it was not copied from the code's output or rebuilt with its algorithm.

The fixture writes watch.json with a completedAt timestamp on phases.watching, and the expected values (recoverable false, watchingComplete true) follow from that input and the rule that a finished watch can't be recovered, not from the code's output.

The stubbed CreateFileW returns a valid handle (42), and the expected ("clear", None) follows from the documented Windows rule that a successful exclusive open means nothing else holds the file, so it is not copied from the implementation's output.

The expected values are hand-written literal strings that equal the inputs. They come from the octal-escape rules the test spells out in its comments ('8' is not an octal digit, and a truncated escape stays as written), not from anything the decoder outputs.

The expected values are written out by hand: the nested path comes from the `.hg` fixture the test builds, and the literal strings ("non-Git VCS state is not independently verified" and "vcs-state-unverified") are hardcoded rather than computed with the implementation's own logic.

The expected string is a hand-written literal built from the `root` path the test set up itself, where it created a `.svn` marker, so it states the intended result for that scenario rather than calling or reproducing the implementation's logic.

Each expected value is a literal you can read directly off its input branch name (e.g. feat/42-new-rule gives 42, and feat/just-a-feature gives empty output with exit 1), so it comes from the branch-naming convention rather than from the parser's output.

The expected content string 'deployment_status completed (acme/repo)' and the meta fields (event, repo, sender, action) are hand-written literals that come straight from the event name and payload fields given in the test, not computed with the router's own code.

The expected values come from inputs the test builds by hand rather than from the script's output: the comment IDs are fixed by its own fake gh state (it starts numbering at 100, and the seeded comments 9/31 and 77/88 test which one becomes canonical); the exit codes 2–14 follow the documented exit-code contract; and the flag forms (-F body=@ versus -f body=) and stderr phrases are stated directly as requirements, not recomputed with the upsert script's own logic.

Each expected outcome (exit 0 or 'PORTABILITY: FAIL', the flagged token, the missing default, the escape path, the wrong @behavior id, the machine-local path) comes from a hand-built fixture that deliberately plants or omits one specific violation, so the verdict comes from how the fixture was designed rather than from recomputing the script's logic, even though the surrounding message wording matches the script's output text.

The expected values (two outcomes, both Passed=true) come straight from the test's own setup: it registers two validators and the stubs it wrote return passed=true, so none of them are taken from the pipeline's output or its algorithm.

The expected values (count 1, Passed false, and validator2 never called) come from what short-circuiting means and from the stub's own failed outcome set in the test, not from output copied from the pipeline's code.

The expected value is an empty output for paths the fixture repo never committed. That follows from the stated rule that a path needs history in HEAD to be flagged, not from anything the hook printed, and the changed lines 366-367 are only the comment stating that rule.

Line 34 only sets the input endpoint and the grpc protocol, and the assertions (no problems, provider enabled, exactly one shutdown hook) follow from the test's own setup, where only traces are enabled through the reviewed export config while the environment says disabled, so they are not copied from the code's output or rebuilt with its algorithm.

The expected result of no diagnostics is set by the test author from the rule's spec: a class that doesn't implement IExposeTools shouldn't be flagged. It isn't copied from the analyzer's output or worked out with the analyzer's own logic.

The expected values are hand-written literals (false, false, false, false, null) that encode the stated design rule that X has no comments and uses only the cookies file for auth, with no browser-cookie fallback; nothing is computed by or copied from the adapter's output.

The expected null comes from the stated rule that an X adapter must not classify YouTube-specific or bare cookie-hint stderr lines, and the test feeds it hand-written literal inputs rather than anything computed from the adapter's pattern table.

The expected STATUS_URL is a hand-written literal (`https://x.com/someuser/status/1720000000000000000`), so it states independently what the canonical form of the raw mobile.twitter.com URL should be, rather than being computed by the adapter's own normalization code.

The expected values (ok false, status "invalid-url", spawn never called) are hand-written literals. They encode the rule that a profile URL like https://x.com/someuser is not a status URL and must be rejected before any spawn, and none of them is computed from or copied out of the adapter's output.

The expected values are hand-written literal phrases ('safety.md', '--autopilot-merge-tier', a negative check on '<snapshotted-head-sha>', push-discipline wording) that encode the contract described in the test's own comment (#675: point at safety.md, don't inline a base-only merge command), not values computed from or derived by the code under test.

The expected values are hand-written literal phrases that the test requires to appear in safety.md; they match that document word for word, but nothing in the block or its fixtures shows whether they came from an independent spec (such as issue #601) or were copied from the document under test, and the test's real weakness is structural: it only checks that the substrings are present.

The expected values are hand-written marker phrases (e.g. 'fail-closed', 'trusted seam', 'operators keep `--merge human-only` on launch lines') that pin required design concepts in the babysit-loop SKILL.md and its reference spoke; they are not computed by any code, and the changed lines only reformat how the reference file's path is built.

The expected exit codes (2 when a destructive git subcommand is blocked, 0 when a read-only one is allowed) come from the hook's stated safety policy and git's documented global-option syntax (`git -h`), not from the hook's output; the changed lines are only comments that restate that policy.
